title: 22. Interview: Netflix — Video Streaming Platform (deep dive)
summary: Interview Q&A for Netflix — Video Streaming Platform (deep dive) — 15 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 15 Netflix — Video Streaming Platform (deep dive) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: 15 Interview Questions with Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: How does Netflix handle 100M+ concurrent streams?

**Answer:** (1) **Open Connect CDN** — 1000+ embedded appliances at ISPs. 95%+ traffic served from edge (not origin). (2) **Adaptive bitrate** — clients auto-adjust quality. (3) **Microservices** — 700+ services on AWS, independently scalable. (4) **Cache layers** — EVCache (memcached), CDN caching. (5) **Regional failover** — active-active across AWS regions.

### Q2: How does Netflix's recommendation system work?

**Answer:** Multi-algorithm approach: (1) **Collaborative filtering** — users who watched X also watched Y. (2) **Content-based** — match genres, actors, descriptions. (3) **Context-aware** — time of day, device, recent activity. (4) **Deep learning** — neural networks for personalized ranking. (5) **A/B testing** — every algorithm change tested on millions of users. 80% of what people watch comes from recommendations.

### Q3: Explain adaptive bitrate streaming.

**Answer:** Video encoded at multiple quality levels (360p to 4K). Client monitors: (1) Available bandwidth, (2) Buffer level, (3) Device capability. Algorithm dynamically switches quality per segment (4-second chunks). Low bandwidth → lower quality (no buffering). High bandwidth → higher quality. Key: avoid oscillation between qualities. Netflix uses per-title encoding — optimal bitrate per content complexity.

### Q4: What is Open Connect?

**Answer:** Netflix's custom CDN. Instead of using commercial CDNs (Akamai), Netflix places hardware (OCA boxes) directly in ISP data centers. Benefits: (1) Lower latency (content is at your ISP), (2) Reduces ISP backbone traffic, (3) Netflix controls the hardware/software. Popular content pre-positioned during off-peak hours. Serves 95%+ of all traffic.

### Q5: How does Netflix handle microservice failures?

**Answer:** (1) **Circuit breaker (Hystrix)** — stop calling failing service, use fallback. (2) **Fallbacks** — cached data, default responses, degraded experience. (3) **Retries with backoff** — transient failures. (4) **Timeouts** — never wait indefinitely. (5) **Bulkheads** — isolate resources per service. (6) **Chaos engineering (Chaos Monkey)** — randomly kill services in production to test resilience.

### Q6: How would you design the video upload pipeline?

**Answer:** (1) Studio uploads raw file (4K, ~100GB). (2) Store in S3. (3) Trigger encoding DAG (Titus scheduler). (4) Analyze complexity → generate encoding ladder. (5) Encode into 10-20 profiles × multiple codecs. (6) Segment into 4-second chunks. (7) Generate DASH manifest. (8) Quality checks (VMAF score). (9) Push to Open Connect during off-peak. Total time: hours per title.

### Q7: How does Netflix A/B test?

**Answer:** Every user is in multiple experiments simultaneously. (1) User ID → hash → variant assignment. (2) Track engagement metrics per variant. (3) Statistical significance testing. (4) Metrics: streaming hours, retention, signup conversion. Netflix runs 250+ experiments concurrently. Even the artwork (thumbnails) is A/B tested — different artwork shown to different user segments.

### Q8: How would you design the search functionality?

**Answer:** (1) **Elasticsearch** for full-text search. (2) **Fuzzy matching** — handle typos. (3) **Personalized ranking** — same query, different results per user. (4) **Autocomplete** — prefix search with popular completions. (5) **Search by everything** — title, actor, director, genre, description. (6) **Index**: content metadata + user signals for ranking.

### Q9: How does Netflix handle data at scale?

**Answer:** (1) **Cassandra** — user data, watch history (high write, eventually consistent). (2) **MySQL** — billing, account data (ACID). (3) **Elasticsearch** — search. (4) **Redis/EVCache** — session, caching. (5) **S3** — video storage. (6) **Spark** — data processing, ML pipeline. (7) **Kafka** — event streaming. Data volumes: hundreds of PB of video, trillions of events/day.

### Q10: How would you implement continue watching across devices?

**Answer:** (1) Client reports progress every 30 seconds to server. (2) Store: `{user_id, content_id, progress_pct, timestamp, device}` in Cassandra. (3) On any device open: query latest progress per content. (4) Conflict resolution: use most recent timestamp. (5) Continue Watching row: query in-progress items, sorted by last watched. Key: lightweight progress updates (not full video state).

### Q11: How does Netflix handle peak traffic (e.g., new season drop)?

**Answer:** (1) **CDN pre-positioning** — popular content pushed to OCAs before release. (2) **Auto-scaling** — more API servers during peak. (3) **Progressive rollout** — stagger release by region. (4) **Graceful degradation** — disable non-essential features. (5) **Load shedding** — reject lowest-priority requests. (6) **Predictive scaling** — ML predicts traffic patterns.

### Q12: How would you design Netflix's notification system?

**Answer:** Event types: new season, recommended, "continue watching" reminder. Architecture: (1) Event triggers → Kafka. (2) Notification router: check user preferences, frequency caps. (3) Channel selection: push (APNS/FCM), email, in-app. (4) Personalization: different message per user. (5) Timing: ML model predicts best time to send. (6) Rate limiting: no spam.

### Q13: How does Netflix ensure content security (DRM)?

**Answer:** (1) **Widevine (Google)** — Android, Chrome. (2) **FairPlay (Apple)** — iOS, Safari. (3) **PlayReady (Microsoft)** — Edge, Windows. Protocol: (1) Client requests license. (2) License server checks subscription. (3) Returns decryption key (bound to device). (4) Content encrypted at rest (AES-128). (5) Watermarking — invisible marks to trace leaks.

### Q14: How would you design Netflix for global scale?

**Answer:** (1) **Multi-region** — AWS us-east, eu-west, ap-southeast. (2) **Data replication** — Cassandra multi-DC replication. (3) **DNS routing** — route users to nearest region. (4) **Open Connect** — edge caches in 160+ countries. (5) **Regional catalog** — different content per country (licensing). (6) **Failover** — if region goes down, redirect to another.

### Q15: Explain Netflix's Chaos Engineering approach.

**Answer:** Deliberately inject failures in production to test resilience. Tools: (1) **Chaos Monkey** — kills random instances. (2) **Chaos Kong** — simulates region failure. (3) **Latency Monkey** — adds artificial latency. (4) **Conformity Monkey** — finds non-compliant instances. Philosophy: "If you want to find vulnerabilities, break things on purpose." Results: Netflix survived AWS outages with minimal impact while competitors went down.

**Next Chapter: [Design Uber →](03_Uber.md)**
